body.text: Aboriginal corporation split over vote to remove family group due to adoption
In short:
The board of Aboriginal corporation Djaara has suggested cancelling the membership of the Dunolly-Lee family, angering family members and peers.
The issue centres around the adoption of Deborah Dunolly, even though Djaara traditional owners confirmed in 2013 that descendants could have traditional owner status even if they were adopted.
What's next?
The vote will go to Djaara's membership at a special general meeting this week.
Central Victorian traditional owner group Djaara is in the midst of a factional divide amid questions that a whole family group is not connected by ancestry to the Aboriginal clan.
WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the names of people who have died, used with the permission of their family.

Several board directors are believed to have resigned amid claims that other directors are trying to oust the Dunolly-Lee family from the Dja Dja Wurrung Clans Aboriginal Corporation, known as Djaara.
At two weeks old, Deborah Dunolly was adopted by Djaara man Thomas Clarence Lynch Dunolly and his wife Rosemary Dawn Dunolly.
"My father gave me his name and an identity I have carried with pride ever since," she wrote in a statement to members ahead of the vote.
"My connection to this Country does not just sit with this membership; it has been a part of my life and who I am for as long as I can remember."
The Dunolly-Lee family declined to be interviewed for this story.
Djaara's chair Rebecca Philips said the board was legally required to maintain an accurate register of traditional owners and, when eligibility concerns arose, put them to a vote by its members.

But members of the Dunolly family group said the Dunolly-Lee family met all the requirements set out in Djaara's rule book about who was a traditional owner, calling the vote a personal attack against the family by other groups.
A special general meeting will take place on Saturday for the roughly 750 Djaara members to vote on whether to cancel the Dunolly-Lee family's membership.
The Dja Dja Wurrung Clans Aboriginal Corporation is the largest registered Aboriginal party by revenue and assets in Victoria, earning nearly $40 million and employing 250 people.
Board proposes membership cancellation
A letter sent by Djaara to its members raised cancelling the membership of 10 people from the Dunolly-Lee family.
"We have noted the underlying disharmony felt by the variation of knowledge, awareness and position on this matter of recognition and eligibility for membership," Ms Phillips wrote.
"They are not a judgement of any person's worth, contribution, family relationships, or sense of belonging within the Dja Dja Wurrung community, as these are independent of membership.
"Notices of intended cancellation were issued, and written objections were received."
The vote on whether the Dunolly-Lee family retains membership will be decided by the organisation's current rule book, the letter read.

But the rule book, finalised in 2013 when Djaara's recognition and settlement agreement was authorised, shows the organisation's full group confirmed the Dunolly-Lee family's rights were inherited from ancestors despite being adopted.
The decision is also backed by minutes from the meeting and emails that specifically mention the Dunolly family's situation.
Deborah Dunolly's statement tells of how her parents were unable to have children of their own and so adopted her and her brother, Thomas.
She also explains how she and her brother were raised within Djaara kinship structures.
Vote goes against rule book, elders say
The board's letter said it was up to members to decide whether they socially recognised and accepted the Dunolly-Lee family members.
Four elders have told the ABC they were "disgusted" by the actions of the board and said they believed Djaara was no longer the gold standard for Aboriginal corporations in Australia.
A Djaara elder, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, told the ABC the vote to cancel the membership of the Dunolly-Lee family went against the organisation's rule book.
Uncle Tommy Baksh, the elder Dunolly member, said the vote to remove the Dunolly-Lee family had left him angry and shocked.
"It's racism, and they're singling out a family that they don't know the full history,"
he said.
"To see them go through the ups and downs of the meetings has been emotional and upsetting."
The rule book is the Djaara's primary internal governing document.
The Dunolly-Lee family has been invited to address the membership at the meeting and make a case for their right to a cultural claim and to remain members.
The Dja Dja Wurrung people are made up of 18 family groups across central Victoria.
Cultural principles and heritage
It was only a year ago that Djaara put a vote to members about who could be a member through cultural claim, with the group deciding to keep to the rule book as it was set out.

A senior Djaara member, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of backlash from Djaara's board, told the ABC that in 2025 the board tried to change the rules, including removing cultural adoption, but the majority of members voted to keep the rule book as it was.
Board minutes from last year show the motion to change the rule book was not carried.
Aunty Marlene "Marl" Burchill remembers Thomas Dunolly riding his bicycle from Cummeragunja to spend the day with her mother, Iris Atkinson.
She said going against the rule book to remove the Dunolly-Lee family from the Aboriginal corporation was "pathetic".
"It's just plain spitefulness and jealousy that's taking place here. Bec has overstepped her position as chair," Ms Burchill said.
"They don't know what good governance is."
She said the vote was a personal attack on the Dunolly family by several other family groups, who she claimed did not have legitimate ties to the Djaara people through a distant relative.
Multiple university Indigenous studies faculties declined to speak publicly about the vote and divide in Djaara.
Families' claims under scrutiny
Djaara's rules set out four elements for being considered a Dja Dja Wurrung person.

These are being a descendant by birth or cultural adoption, the person identifying as Dja Dja Wurrung, having an active association with Dja Dja Wurrung business and country, and being accepted by other Djaara traditional owners.
The final point clarifies that being accepted can be achieved by being a member or by meeting the first two elements of birth and cultural adoption, and self-identifying.

Documents show the full group of the organisation in 2013 decided to respect the ancestors' decision about who could claim cultural connection, meaning the Dunolly-Lee family could be a traditional owner, even though their claim is through being adopted.
But the division within the organisation has also raised questions about whether other members are rightful descendants.

Documents question whether some Dja Dja Wurrung members are rightful descendants of Caroline Malcolm, and not her husband's second wife, Maryanne, who was from country further east in the Goulburn area.
The rule book states that Caroline Malcolm's mother was born in 1846 at Menzies Station Loddon, and may have been recorded in the Mount Franklinford 1863 census as residing at Bullock Creek.
It said a Coranderrk Mission burial registry lists Caroline Malcolm's family group as being from the Loddon area.
Ms Phillips is the head representative for the Caroline Malcolm family group — one of 18 family groups that make up the 18 available seats on Djaara's board.

A Djaara member told the ABC that differences between family groups, Ms Phillips's performance as chair and her family group's eligibility, as well as the Dunolly-Lee issue, had driven several board directors to leave.
In a statement, Ms Phillips said claims regarding widespread director resignations were incorrect, adding that the board held a quorum to operate legally.
"Out of respect for our traditional owner community, procedural fairness and member privacy, we will not comment on individual memberships or internal governance matters through the media," she said.
"Our focus remains firmly on delivering outcomes for our members and caring for Country."
Djaara and Ms Phillips did not respond to questions about Caroline Malcolm's family connections.

By law, the national regulator for Aboriginal corporations, the Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations (ORIC), can appoint a special administrator to take control of an organisation in serious circumstances.
ORIC states it generally only places organisations into special administration when there is a risk of failure or severe dysfunction.
In a statement, ORIC said it did not make public comment on whether it was considering, monitoring or investigating a particular matter.
"This approach helps ensure the integrity of our regulatory processes and protects the interests of those involved," it said.
